question: An anaesthesiologist is called to provide sedation for a patient undergoing an MRI scan. Which of the following represents the most significant additional hazard specific to this non-operating room anaesthesia (NORA) setting?

answers.text: The patient is likely to be more anxious than in the operating theatre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Patient anxiety is not specific to NORA; it is a universal consideration in all anaesthetic settings.

answers.text: The strong magnetic field precludes use of standard ferromagnetic anaesthetic equipment, monitoring leads, and infusion pumps unless MRI-compatible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The powerful magnetic field of the MRI scanner can cause ferromagnetic objects to become projectiles, interfere with electronic equipment, and disable non-MRI-compatible monitoring — all life-threatening hazards unique to this NORA setting.

answers.text: Oxygen is unavailable outside the operating theatre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oxygen must be available in all NORA settings — providing oxygen supply is a NORA prerequisite, not an inherent unavailability.

answers.text: Neuromuscular blocking drugs cannot be used outside the operating theatre

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Neuromuscular blocking drugs can be used in NORA settings when indicated, provided appropriate monitoring and reversal are available.

overallFeedback.feedback: The defining hazard of MRI-based NORA is the powerful magnetic field that renders all standard ferromagnetic anaesthetic equipment (laryngoscopes, pumps, monitors) potentially dangerous or non-functional.

Exactly right. MRI is the most hazard-dense NORA environment due to the magnetic field — only MRI-compatible (MR-conditional) equipment can be used; standard ferromagnetic devices become dangerous projectiles.
